content: Retapamulin is a topical medication used to treat impetigo, a bacterial skin infection caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) or Streptococcus pyogenes. It is applied as a thin layer to the affected area, up to 100 cm², twice daily for five days. For children under nine months of age, the safety and efficacy of this medication have not been established. For those aged nine months and older, it can be applied to affected areas covering up to 2% of the body surface area, twice daily for five days. This medication is not intended for oral, intranasal, ophthalmic, or intravaginal use, as its safety and efficacy on mucosal surfaces have not been established. If sensitization or severe local irritation occurs, the treatment should be discontinued. Epistaxis (nosebleeds) has been reported when used on nasal mucosa. There is no data available on its use in pregnant women to assess risks of birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Similarly, there is no data on the presence of the drug in human breast milk or its effects on breastfed infants or milk production. However, due to negligible systemic absorption, breastfeeding is not expected to expose the infant to the drug. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the medication and any potential adverse effects on the infant. Retapamulin works as a pleuromutilin antibacterial agent by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. It is bacteriostatic at minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) and bactericidal at 1000 times the MIC. The drug has low systemic absorption, is 94% protein-bound, and is metabolized in vitro by the liver enzyme CYP3A4. Common side effects include mild burning, stinging, or itching at the application site. Prolonged or repeated use may lead to secondary infections, such as fungal infections. Serious allergic reactions are rare. If side effects occur, patients in the U.S. should contact their doctor for medical advice, while those in Canada should do the same. Before using retapamulin, patients should inform their doctor or pharmacist if they are allergic to it or have other allergies. The product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly needed. It is unknown if the drug passes into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter the effectiveness of retapamulin or increase the risk of serious side effects. Patients should maintain a list of all medications and supplements they use and share it with their healthcare provider. In case of accidental ingestion or overdose, immediate medical attention should be sought. U.S. residents can contact the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222. If a dose is missed, it should be applied as soon as remembered unless it is close to the time for the next dose. In such cases, the missed dose should be skipped, and the next dose applied at the regular time. The medication should be stored at room temperature and discarded properly when expired or no longer needed. It should not be flushed down the toilet or poured into a drain unless instructed to do so. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about the product. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Patients should always consult their healthcare provider for complete information tailored to their specific health needs.
